To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the proteasome can be immobilized at metal interfaces via fusion of affinity tags at the pore or at the side, that the proteasomes with the fusion tag around the pore aperture are functional and that the proteasomal degradation is a two‐stroke process with two substrates bound in antechambers.

(1) one pore is sufficient to allow for substrate entry and for product release, (2) the two antechambers of the proteasomal core particle are accessible to substrates and (3) the proteasome can associate with two substrate molecules simultaneously.
the proteasome can degrade only one protein at a time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms that govern proteasome activity.
the elucidation of the mechanism of proteasome function by single‐molecule spectroscopy.
the design and characterization of functional proteasome–protein interfaces, which are the key to unraveling the molecular mechanism and the functional role of the proteasomal degradation machinery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 20S core particle is a two‐stroke motor, where each stroke is associated with the degradation of one substrate.
the proteasome is a two‐substrate processing enzyme with a two‐stroke engine.
the 20S is a ‘two‐substrate’ proteasome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proteasome is a highly efficient, yet simple machine.
the proteasome is a highly efficient and versatile proteolytic machine.
a single‐molecule approach to the proteasome has revealed a new level of functional details that could be missed by conventional biochemical approaches.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proteasome is not a ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ machine.
the proteasome is a versatile molecular machine with the capacity to bind and process multiple substrates simultaneously.
single‐molecule spectroscopy provides the means to unravel the mechanism of a complex enzyme at atomic detail, which is not accessible by conventional ensemble‐averaging methods.
